findings.content: `html select` has specificity (0,0,2), which beats the bare `select` rules used by the settings window (`settings.css:86-96` and the light-theme override at `settings.css:201-206`, both specificity (0,0,1)). As a result the settings `<select>` no longer uses its own palette (`#35393b` / `#45494b` / `color: inherit` / `border-radius: 5px`) and, more importantly, the `prefers-color-scheme: light` override stops working: the select keeps the dark `--panel-elev` fallback `#1b1d22` with `#d8d8d8` text inside an otherwise light UI. The file header comment ("without touching colors set by those rules") is therefore inaccurate for element-level rules.
findings.suggestion: Either restrict the shared rule to the arrow/appearance properties only (leaving colors to each window), or keep the color block at plain `select` specificity so per-window `select` rules still win, e.g. move `background-color`/`color`/`border` out of `html select` or guard them with `:where(html) select`.

findings.content: The allowlist used by `validate_skill_path` lives in a process-global `Mutex<Vec<PathBuf>>` that is only populated as a side effect of `skills_list`. This makes the read/write/explain commands order-dependent: `skill_read`/`skill_write` on a repo-local skill fail with "path is outside the known skill roots" if no listing ran before (e.g. after a window reload that restores a previously opened skill), and a later `skills_list` with a different `project_paths` set silently invalidates paths that were valid a moment earlier. It also means the reachable area for writes is decided by whatever unvalidated `project_paths` the frontend last sent, rather than by the argument of the call being authorized. Passing the owning project path explicitly to `skill_read`/`skill_write`/`skill_explain` (and validating it there) would remove both the hidden state and the ordering dependency.

The user-facing description is always pluralized, so an index with a single bullet renders as "Index loaded every session · 1 entries" (the test even asserts that wording). Consider selecting the singular form when `entries == 1`.
findings.anchor: +        return format!("Index loaded every session · {entries} entries");

findings.content: `mountMemoryModal` is an almost line-by-line copy of `mountSkillsModal` (`src/modules/skills-library/skills-modal.ts`): the same state block (`backdrop`, `mode`, `query`, `selectedIdx`, `filtered`, `contentCache`, `previewToken`), the same `loadPreview` / `paintList` / `beginEdit` / `saveEditor` / `backToList` / `open` / `close` flow, and the local `renderRowList`, `updateSelection` and `renderPreview` helpers duplicate `renderSkillList`, `updateSkillSelection` and `renderSkillPreview` from `skills-modal-list.ts`. Two copies of this logic will drift (they already differ: skills `saveEditor` only re-renders, memory reloads the list). Consider extracting the shared list/preview/editor shell into a reusable module parameterised by row type and data source.
findings.suggestion: Extract a shared "library modal" helper (list + preview + editor shell) and build both /skills and /memory on top of it instead of duplicating ~500 lines.

findings.content: `CursorWindow` is structurally identical to the existing `AuthoritativeWindow` (`usedPercent` + `resetsAt`), and the consumers already treat them as the same type: `cursorPlanCard` passes `summary.plan` straight into `authoritativeWindowRow(window: AuthoritativeWindow, …)` and `updateCountdowns` types the cursor windows as `AuthoritativeWindow | null`. Keeping two names for one shape invites divergence.
findings.suggestion: Reuse `AuthoritativeWindow` in `CursorSummary` (or alias `export type CursorWindow = AuthoritativeWindow`).
